catalog_quote: /ə/ represents the vowel of weak syllables in Lan Hmyo, and it has a shorter duration than vowels in strong syllables, with a tendency to assimilate to the vowel of the following strong syllable. In Lan Hmyo, words always carry a strong syllable in the ultimate syllable, with a stress on it. Penultimate syllables do not have a stress, and weak syllables having /ə/ typically appear at this position. Based on the distribution, the author assumes that the morpheme in question has the form taA-, and constitutes a phonological word with the following morpheme. It manifests as təA- before a stressed strong syllable. Therefore, təA- typically occurs as the first syllable of disyllabic words. [p. 177] ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Luopohe Miao is a tone language (three lexical tones A 42, B 55, C 24, plus loan tones B' C'). On top of tone, Taguchi states a fixed word-final stress: the last syllable of every word is a 'strong' (full) syllable and bears the stress; the penultimate syllable is unstressed and is the position where reduced 'weak' syllables (vowel /ə/, short, assimilating to the next vowel; the noun prefixes and proclitic-like morphemes such as taA-/təA-, aA-, muA-) occur. Taguchi's 2016 Japanese phoneme sketch says the same in syllable terms: a weak syllable always precedes a strong syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not called 'secondary', but p. 178 states that an antepenultimate syllable 'can take a stress before an unstressed penultimate syllable' (so taA- keeps its full vowel there), i.e. stresses alternate leftward from the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: The negative marker muA- 'does not take a stress' even in antepenultimate position (p. 178). In four-syllable expressives (Taguchi 2021 fn./§, Stories of Hmyo fn. 93, 115) the second syllable is made prominent and lengthened with a raised B tone and the third is weak, a template that overrides the ordinary pattern. Loanword tones B'/C' do not trigger tone alternations.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (Taguchi treats taA- + host as one phonological word, marked with hyphens for dependent morphemes); most native words are monosyllabic or prefix+root disyllables, so 'final stress' mostly means the root syllable after an unstressed prefix. Elicited/citation data checked with a native consultant (Song Yun); no instrumental study. Chinese sources instead speak of 轻声 (two neutral-tone values 02/05 on noun prefixes, per Chen Qiguang 苗瑶语文 p. 241 via zh.wikipedia), which is the same prefix-weakening phenomenon.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes "Lan Hmyo" (lanB hmøA), the speech of the Hmyo (花苗) people of Gaozhai Township, Kaiyang County and neighbouring Fuquan/Guiding/Longli, i.e. the western dialect of Luopohe Miao; Glottolog files Taguchi's 2002 sketch of the same variety as "Western Luobohe" under luop1235 (ISO hml), and Taguchi himself gives ISO hml for Lan Hmyo. The eastern dialect (Xijia 西家, Kaili; Chen 2007, four tones) is not covered by the statement; Glottolog gives it no separate glottocode.
